title: Kansas and Nebraska complaints against OpenAI (not obtained)
note: Kansas was filed in Shawnee County District Court and Nebraska in Buffalo County District Court (case number D09CI260000488), both per press reporting. Statements about these two states stop at the court name and the statutes named in the announcements.

title: Mont. Code Ann. sections 30-14-2802(6), 30-14-2811(2)(b), 30-14-2819, 30-14-2820(1)
note: Montana Consumer Data Privacy Act as amended by SB 297, effective 2025-10-01. The amendment added the minor provisions and removed the cure period. Section 30-14-2811(2)(b) prohibits using a system design feature to significantly increase, sustain, or extend a minor's use without consent; section 30-14-2802(6) excludes agreements obtained through dark patterns from the definition of consent.

title: Neb. Rev. Stat. sections 87-1302 and 87-1309 (Age-Appropriate Online Design Code Act)
note: Enacted as LB 504 (effective 2026-01-01, attorney general enforcement from 2026-07-01) and amended by LB 838 (effective 2026-07-17), which expanded the covered design feature list from five to eleven and added clause (k): a feature that increases usage through the illusion of talking with a human being that seeks to elicit feelings of intimacy from the user. Penalties run through the Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act, up to 50,000 dollars per violation. Verified through law firm commentary and legal databases; the Nebraska Legislature server could not be reached from this working environment.

title: State consumer protection and child privacy statutes cited in the complaints
note: Arkansas Act 952 (Children and Teens' Online Privacy Protection Act, effective 2026-07-01) and the Arkansas Deceptive Trade Practices Act; Iowa Code sections 714.16(7), 714.16A, and 715D.4(2); Idaho Code section 48-606(1)(e); A.R.S. section 44-1531(A); W. Va. Code chapter 46A article 6. These are the bases for the per-violation civil penalty figures compared in section 3.4.

title: Attorney General Griffin Sues OpenAI for Misleading Arkansans Over Safety of ChatGPT
note: The only announcement that lists nine states, including Utah. The Utah Attorney General's newsroom carries no corresponding announcement.

title: Montana and Nebraska attorney general announcements on the OpenAI filings
note: The Montana notice states that the allegations have not been proven in court. The Nebraska release, read through a syndicated reprint, names the Nebraska Consumer Protection Act, the Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act, and the Age-Appropriate Online Design Code Act.

title: Strengthening ChatGPT's responses in sensitive conversations
note: Source of the before and after compliance figures for self-harm (77 to 91 percent), emotional reliance (50 to 97 percent), and psychosis or mania (27 to 92 percent) on a roughly 1,000-conversation challenging evaluation set, and of the population prevalence figures (0.15 percent of weekly active users versus 0.05 percent of messages for explicit suicide-planning signals). The same announcement reports inter-rater agreement as a 71 to 77 percent range. The page returned an access error during writing and was read through a Wayback Machine capture.

title: Ads in ChatGPT (help center) and A milestone in expanding access to AI
note: The help center document states that ads are not shown to accounts identified as belonging to users under 18, based on account-level age information and age prediction where available. The August 2026 post is the company's own disclosure of ChatGPT advertising revenue.

title: ChatGPT for Teens
note: Launched 18 August 2026 for users aged 13 to 17. Accounts are routed into the teen experience automatically by age assurance, which draws on stated age, account history and usage patterns rather than up-front verification; adults misclassified into it can restore full access through selfie-based age verification. Cited in section 4.1 as evidence that the stated/predicted/verified age classification is operational. The company's own announcement page was unreachable from this environment; confirmed through multiple independent secondary reports.

title: OpenAI's Bid to Allow X-Rated Talk Is Freaking Out Its Own Advisers
note: The sole source for the roughly 12 percent age-prediction misclassification figure. The West Virginia complaint attributes it to news reports at paragraph 111 but drops that attribution when the figure reappears at paragraph 245(h).

title: The Common Sense Media Census: AI Use by Tweens and Teens, 2026
note: Telephone and online survey of 1,204 children and teens aged 9 to 17, fielded in March 2026. Source of the 58 percent figure for ages 9 to 12, which is self-reported use.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Applications Use Among US Youth
note: Passive sensing of device activity in 6,488 households using a commercial parental monitoring app, covering 2024-09-01 to 2025-04-01. Source of the 20.5 percent figure for ages 10 to 12 that the complaints round to 21 percent. The gap with the Common Sense Media figure is a difference of measurement method, not of age band alone.

title: Towards Reliable Forgetting: A Survey on Machine Unlearning Verification
note: Finds that verifying that data was in fact removed is less settled than the removal techniques themselves, and notes the circularity of verification against a retrained model.

title: Verification of Machine Unlearning is Fragile
note: Shows that unlearning verification can itself be manipulated; data subjects cannot inspect the removal process.

title: Korean child privacy guideline and the 2025 dark pattern amendments
note: Personal Information Protection Commission guideline on children's and adolescents' personal data (2022, a self-assessment document rather than binding law), and the amended Electronic Commerce Act banning six dark pattern types effective 2025-02-14. All six target designs that induce spending; no Korean provision targets designs that extend time spent. The shutdown law that regulated playing time directly was repealed in August 2021. Statutory text was not read verbatim, so the article names these instruments rather than citing article numbers.

title: Doe v. OpenAI Foundation and other adjacent proceedings
authority: U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California
note: Federal class action filed one day before the state suits, pleading that training models on minors' data is itself the wrong and seeking a share of the value created. Distinct from the state actions, which plead per-violation civil penalties. Also distinct: New York Times v. OpenAI in the Southern District of New York (log preservation order), Florida's separate June 2026 suit, and Utah v. Snap (June 2026), which included claims about a chatbot feature.
